## What we covered

We finished the two slides left over from the hospital-price class, price
transparency and competition, and then started on the pricing itself. A hospital
with price-setting power, a hospital that simply takes the price it's given, and
the beginning of the case where it faces both at once. The first fifteen minutes
went to your questions about the exam.

## Key points

- Price transparency sounds obvious and isn't. Start with what you'd actually
  have to post. A vet can put a chart on the wall because the service is known in
  advance and the price is the same for everyone. Walk into an emergency
  department and neither holds. Nobody knows yet which of twenty things is wrong
  with you, finding out is itself most of what gets billed, and the price depends
  on who your insurer is. Even if we solved all of that, acting on the number is
  a separate problem. You don't know what treatment you need, a lot of care isn't
  planned, your network restricts where you can go, and a cheaper hospital you
  have to reach by ambulance isn't cheaper. Transparency can also push the wrong
  way for some people. If the lowest posted price is already past what you can
  pay and you're uninsured, the number deters you from going at all. Forgone care
  is real.
- Posted prices can raise prices, and whether they do depends on who gets to see
  them. If prices are visible to patients only, and patients respond, you get the
  story you'd expect, competition for the cheaper option. If they're visible to
  the whole market, I can walk into a negotiation and say you're paying the
  hospital across town more than you're paying me for the same service, so pay me
  that. Nothing there requires coordination. It follows straight from the
  bargaining model. What turns it off is a patient who actually uses the
  information, and we have good reasons to doubt that, since insurance absolves
  you of most of the difference, the tools are hard to use, and much of the
  decision isn't yours anyway. Economists said this before the rule existed
  rather than after, and the clearest precedent, posted prices in the Danish
  concrete market, saw prices rise. How the rule was written then mattered as much
  as that it passed. Hospitals have to post in both a machine-readable and a
  consumer-friendly format, and what they produced was thousands of unlabeled
  codes spread across spreadsheets and JSON files, with some posting nothing at
  all for years before any fine arrived. Compliance is better now and still
  incomplete, and the quality is poor enough that an industry exists to scrape
  these files, clean them, and sell the result back. A disclosure rule is only as
  good as the format it specifies and the enforcement behind it.
- More competition usually lowers prices, but not when firms compete on more than
  price. If patients are very responsive to quality and barely responsive to
  price, then competing means competing on quality, and quality has to be paid
  for, so more competition can raise the price. That isn't a reason to think
  competition doesn't matter here. We allocate health care through a market and
  then don't supply the market with much competition, which is the worst of the
  two arrangements. The Fort Wayne reading is the case study. One system bought up
  the hospitals and physician practices around it and raised prices continuously,
  with no competitor to stop it and insurers who couldn't walk away from the only
  hospital in town.
- A hospital with price-setting power is the firm you already know, and we don't
  need a separate model for not-for-profits. You can write one down, utility over
  profit from private insurers, profit from public payers, and the quantity of
  care delivered, but you can't solve it without knowing how much weight sits on
  each piece, so it predicts nothing. We assume profit maximization for everyone
  instead. Then it's marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and price up to the
  demand curve. With inverse demand $p = 16 - q$ and costs $c(q) = 5 + q^{2}$,
  write profit as $(16-q)q - 5 - q^{2}$, differentiate to get $16 - 4q = 0$, so
  $q = 4$, $p = 12$, marginal cost is 8, and the markup is 4, or fifty percent.
  Work from the profit function rather than memorizing marginal revenue. You
  won't always be able to see what the marginal revenue function is, and the
  derivative never changes. Two things to carry. Marginal revenue falls faster
  than demand because selling one more unit means dropping the price for
  everyone, not just the marginal buyer, and if you could price-discriminate
  perfectly the two would be the same line. And a pure price taker has a flat
  marginal revenue curve, which is the whole model: marginal revenue is the money
  you get for the next unit of care, an outside payer has fixed that number, so
  only your cost curve shapes the decision. That is not capitation. Under
  capitation the revenue is fixed in total and each additional unit of care
  reduces your profit.
- Put the two together and you get a kinked marginal revenue curve, which is the
  one new idea. Picture two lines of patients at the door, one commercial and one
  Medicare, and take them in order of marginal revenue. The commercial patients
  start above the Medicare price, so you serve them first, and at the point where
  commercial marginal revenue has fallen to the Medicare price you switch lines.
  Marginal revenue slopes down and then goes flat. Total quantity is still where
  marginal revenue meets marginal cost, you just have to know which branch you're
  standing on, which makes this a logic problem on top of a derivative problem.
  The private quantity is where the two marginal revenue curves meet, the gap up
  to the total is the public quantity, and the private price comes from pricing up
  to demand at the private quantity, not at the total. Now cut the Medicare price.
  The kink moves right, the private quantity rises, and the private price falls.
  The reason is clearer in patients than in curves. A Medicare patient just became
  less valuable, you'd rather fill that slot with a commercial patient, and the
  only way to attract one more commercial patient is to charge less. That is the
  opposite of cost shifting, which is the hospital industry's claim that cutting
  Medicare rates forces them to raise commercial prices to make up the
  difference. Keep cost shifting separate from cross-subsidization, which is
  funding a money-losing service out of a profitable one, happens routinely, and
  isn't controversial.

## Worth knowing for the exam

The exam is all short answer, no multiple choice. Every question comes in four or
five parts, and a couple of those parts will be a number, maybe a graph, and then
a short discussion of what you found. The setup will look like what we write on
the board. Here's a benefit function, here's a constraint, here's an outside
option, now find the optimum.

The difficulty is the difficulty of the in-class problems and the worksheets on
the website. Work through all of them. Any review I hand out is a version of
those with the numbers changed, a utility function to the one-third instead of a
square root. Nothing new will appear.

There's more on you this term than there used to be, and it's worth knowing why.
The homework used to carry theory questions as well as empirical ones, and
take-home theory stopped being useful once everyone could get a perfect answer
without doing it. So the homework is empirical now, and the quizzes are too short
to hold a real derivation, which means nothing has forced you to practice the
computations. The material is all covered. The practice is yours to go get.

Come talk to me or the TA, and come with something specific. I worked this
problem, I got this answer, I don't see where it went wrong. That's a
conversation. What's on the exam isn't.

On grading, roughly three points a question, zero for blank or for restating the
question, one point for a real start that doesn't get there. Partial credit is
discrete, so don't expect fractions of a point. It's on paper, one part per page,
and you won't need all the pages. If you find yourself writing an essay, you've
gone wrong. Explain the intuition of your answer, not the mechanics of taking a
derivative. You can bring your own formula sheet.
